title: Please include a higher `timeout=` option in `install_torch()` to prevent download file 60s timeout
description:
Hello, 

Initial `library(torch)` or manual `install_torch()` very often fails due to large file download timeout, as mentionned by https://github.com/mlverse/torch/issues/186#issuecomment-735576520

### Current situation
Usual home internet connection do not succeed to download libtorch (130MB+ ) before the default `timeout=60`, making the first contact with the package frustrating, and diverting the user from the goal to build and train a neural network.

Even if problem is made explicit during the `install_torch()` process by the log : 
```(r)
Warning messages:
1: In utils::download.file(library_url, temp_file) :
  downloaded length 44901568 != reported length 141774525
2: In utils::download.file(library_url, temp_file) :
  URL 'https://download.pytorch.org/libtorch/cpu/libtorch-macos-1.7.1.zip': Timeout of 60 seconds was reached
3: Failed to install Torch, manually run install_torch(). download from 'https://download.pytorch.org/libtorch/cpu/libtorch-macos-1.7.1.zip' failed 
```
But it is not obvious for most users on how to increase the timeout with the global `options(timeout = 360)`

## Proposed improvement
add a `timeout=360` option in the `install_torch()` function so that
- solution to the problem is self contained in the documentation
- an adapted default value gives a much higher success-rate of initial installation 

Thanks a lot

title: Complex dtype
description:
Hi! I noticed from `dtype.R` that `cdouble` is the same as `cfloat64`.
```
torch_cfloat <- function() torch_dtype$new(cpp_torch_cfloat())
torch_cfloat32 <- function() torch_dtype$new(cpp_torch_cfloat())
torch_cdouble <- function() torch_dtype$new(cpp_torch_cdouble())
torch_cfloat64 <- function() torch_dtype$new(cpp_torch_cdouble())
```

In pytorch they use `cdouble` as the same as `torch.complex128` (2 `torch.float64` values). Are the names really supposed to be different from pytorch? It confused me a little when I saw that as I didn't know if `cfloat64` was representing 2 32 bit values or 64 bits for each value. So I went to check on pytorch's documentation, which made it clear (2nd print).
Also, I don't know if intentional or not, I think this torch package is missing the `torch.complex32` (`chalf`) implementation.

title: missing torch_size
description:
Hello!

in Python: 
`
>>> torch.rand(10).shape
torch.Size([10])
`
in R:
`
> torch_rand(10)$shape
[1] 10
`
So while Python gives us a torch.Size, R just gives an integer. This leads to problems further down the road when I sample from a distribution
`
distr_normal(0,1)$sample(10)
`
is different to the python
`
torch.distributions.Normal(0,1).sample(torch.Size([10]))
`
The sample function in Python does not accept integers at all, but it only accepts torch.Size([]) values. This breaks any translation attempt where a sample is drawn.

Will torch_size be implemented in the future, or is there a better way to do this? 
Thanks!

title: Using JIT operators without writing wrappers
description:
In python one can do something like:

```
import torch
torch.ops.load_library("build/libwarp_perspective.so")
print(torch.ops.my_ops.warp_perspective(torch.randn(32, 32), torch.rand(3, 3)))
```

In R, we have an equivalent for `torch.ops.load_library` but we can't really use the operations without writing C++ wrappers for them. We should be able to generate the wrappers using JIT types automatically, so users could do `ops$my_ops$warp_perspective` and access the operator with the JIT signature.

See more info [here](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/advanced/torch_script_custom_ops.html#using-the-torchscript-custom-operator-in-python)

title: Dataloader drops dimensions
description:
Hello,

I've noticed the dataloader simplifies/drops dimensions if they equal 1, which is unexpected.

In particular, if the number of observations in a sampled batch equals one, the "batch" dimension will be simplified.

Example:

    ds <- tensor_dataset(torch_rand(11,3), torch_rand(11,1))
    loader <- dataloader(ds, batch_size=10, shuffle=TRUE)
    coro::loop(for (b in loader) {
        print(b[[1]]$shape)
    })

outputs:

    [1] 10  3
    [1] 3

instead of what would be expected:

    [1] 10  3
    [1] 1 3

I haven't investigated whether it's specifically from the dataloader, or if it inherits this behaviour from another function (that might not be supposed to simplify either).

title: torch_split much slower than equivalent function in pytorch
description:
Hi @dfalbel,

I'm encountering a huge difference in performance when using ```torch_split``` in R and in pytorch. 

Here's an example using R where ```torch_split``` takes about 25-30 seconds:

```R
library(torch)
nSubjects <- 75e3
nFeatures <- 1e3
torch::torch_manual_seed(seed=42)

rowIds <- torch::torch_randint(1,nSubjects, c(1e6,1))
columnIds <- torch::torch_randint(1,nFeatures, c(1e6, 1))

tensor <- torch::torch_cat(c(rowIds, columnIds), dim=2)

sortedTensor <- tensor$sort(dim=1)[[1]]

counts <- as.integer(torch::torch_unique_consecutive(sortedTensor[,1], return_counts=TRUE)[[3]])

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(splitted <- torch::torch_split(sortedTensor[,2], counts), times=1)
```

In python the split function for the same example takes about 0.5 seconds. 

```Python
import torch
torch.manual_seed(seed=42)
nSubjects = int(75e3)
nFeatures = int(1e3)

rowIds = torch.randint(0, nSubjects, (int(1e6), 1))
columnIds = torch.randint(1, nFeatures, (int(1e6), 1))

tensor = torch.cat((rowIds, columnIds), dim=1)
sortedTensor = tensor.sort(dim=1)[1]

counts = torch.unique_consecutive(sortedTensor[:, 0], return_counts=True)[1].tolist()
splitted = torch.split(sortedTensor[:, 1], counts)

```

I assume these are calling the same libtorch functions under the hood? Any idea for the difference in performance?

I'm using torch 0.9 and pytorch 1.13.

title: Deep Cloning of modules
description:
I am trying to figure out a way to create a deep clone of a torch module. 
While trying out different approaches  I discovered some unexpected behavior that I am documenting here. 

The tricky part about creating the deep clone is to preserve reference semantics. 
Therefore I picked the otherwise randomly seeming example below, where a deep clone should preserve the references, i.e. that weight1 and weight2 point to the same parameter. 

``` r
library(torch)

nn_custom = nn_module("nn_custom",
  initialize = function() {
    w = nn_parameter(torch_randn(1, 1))
    self$weight1 = w
    self$weight2 = w
  }
)

net = nn_custom()


# This returns only weight1
net$named_parameters(TRUE)
#> $weight1
#> torch_tensor
#> -2.2368
#> [ CPUFloatType{1,1} ][ requires_grad = TRUE ]
# This returns weight1 and weight2
net$named_parameters(FALSE)
#> $weight1
#> torch_tensor
#> -2.2368
#> [ CPUFloatType{1,1} ][ requires_grad = TRUE ]
#> 
#> $weight2
#> torch_tensor
#> -2.2368
#> [ CPUFloatType{1,1} ][ requires_grad = TRUE ]

# This does not work, because `$register_parameter()` is not called.
# I would expect it to work though or at least throw a warning
net$weight1 = torch_clone(net$weight1) + 1000
net$weight1
#> torch_tensor
#> -2.2368
#> [ CPUFloatType{1,1} ][ requires_grad = TRUE ]
# This does work
net$weight1 = nn_parameter(torch_clone(net$weight1) + 1000)
net$weight1
#> torch_tensor
#>  997.7632
#> [ CPUFloatType{1,1} ][ grad_fn = <AddBackward1> ]

# Also I was surprised to observe the following:
net = nn_custom()
net1 = net$clone(deep = TRUE)

state = lapply(net1$state_dict(), function(x) nn_parameter(torch_clone(x) + 1000))

net1$load_state_dict(state)

net$weight1
#> torch_tensor
#>  1001.7814
#> [ CPUFloatType{1,1} ][ requires_grad = TRUE ]
net1$weight1
#> torch_tensor
#>  1001.7814
#> [ CPUFloatType{1,1} ][ requires_grad = TRUE ]
```

<sup>Created on 2023-01-24 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

title: `named_parameters` error when multiple references
description:
```
# This returns only weight1
net$named_parameters(TRUE)
#> $weight1
#> torch_tensor
#> -2.2368
#> [ CPUFloatType{1,1} ][ requires_grad = TRUE ]
# This returns weight1 and weight2
net$named_parameters(FALSE)
```

This is a bug. We should only ever return unique tensors.
We could potentially make it an error to assign the same tensor to multiple names within a module to avoid having to handle this case.

_Originally posted by @dfalbel in https://github.com/mlverse/torch/issues/968#issuecomment-1404826314_

title: Warn when overwriting model parameters
description:
```
# This does not work, because `$register_parameter()` is not called.
# I would expect it to work though or at least throw a warning

I think we should throw a warning here. If a `nn_parameter` already exists with that name, then reassigning a 'non-parameter' to the same name is probably a mistake.

title: torch 0.9.0 and 0.9.1 deadlock when run in parallel
description:
Hi,

Pytorch/libtorch as of version 1.12 allows forking in combination with autograd when only using the CPU and not the GPU as in this issue here https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/69839.

Previously (up until 0.8.1), running torch from R inside mclapply through this package was possible when setting ```torch_set_num_threads(1)```. Now, a deadlock situation emerges when doing so.

I have created a minimal example (similar to as in a previous issue I created) the code is:

```
library(torch)
library(parallel)

testfun <- function (x) {
  lstm <- nn_lstm(50, 50)
  in_data <- torch_tensor(matrix(rnorm(50),1), torch_float())
  out_data <- torch_tensor(array(rnorm(2500), c(1,50,50)), torch_float())
  out_pred <- lstm(in_data)[[1]]
  loss <- nnf_mse_loss(out_pred, out_data)
  loss$backward()
}

mclapply(1:2, testfun)
```

When running this code, a number of threads are spawned, and a deadlock situation where the CPU usage is 0% and the code never completes is created.

The thread tree in htop looks like this:
![Screenshot 2023-01-27 at 11 33 27](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10993608/215068786-5508ad1e-a21a-49d9-b945-28497e56c0d2.png)

Investigating the threads in gdb we can see that there seems to be a lockup in the ```std::condition_variable``` used in lantern/utils.cpp. https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/8369336cc25df518f6791917ad2653661b1f1a28/lantern/src/utils.cpp#L325

We see two threads stuck here:
![cond_var1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10993608/215069812-967ba99b-f0ec-4732-9957-20a3aa3784b6.png)
 
5 threads are stuck here: 
![cond_var3](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10993608/215069915-7973fdd5-af05-4742-b493-827d3d0319ef.png)

And 5 threads stuck in this location:
 ![cond_var9](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10993608/215070010-3795d5c4-b6db-46af-a97d-ab308d0bf29d.png)

There is also one thread in select.c:
![select](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10993608/215070111-608d039a-ea0f-4947-b02d-9aaea6855517.png)

One in nanosleep:
![sleep1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10993608/215070194-b166b6d3-ed21-4f89-9af2-3ace593c8519.png)

Finally, there are two threads stopped in libgomp:
![thread](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/10993608/215070306-d58e3728-df88-46f2-b821-a65d624d85b5.png)

I am unsure about which information may be relevant, and wanted to give a thorough example of the problem, hence the many screenshots. If more information is needed, let me know.

Examining the source between versions 0.8.1 and 0.9.0 I can see that a ```ThreadPool``` was added, and it has the possibly offending ```std::condition_variable```. My suspicion is that the same ```std::condition_variable``` is poked at from multiple threads created by ```mclapply```, which is not the intention as the ```ThreadPool``` will now be locked and unlocked in unintended ways, causing the deadlock.

I can continue debugging, but would love some input in how to proceed, and I think that someone more familiar with the code can probably give better pointers towards where to look. Also I should mention that I am overall very happy with the package, and think that it is really nice to be able to use libtorch so seamlessly from R.

title: Unexpected warning (about resizing) from torch_matrix_exp() only when input tensor values are < 1, despite output being correct

This is consistent across 1000s of calls to `torch_matrix_exp()`: scientifically-notated inputs `x` *always* trigger the warning; non-scientifically-notated inputs `x` *never* trigger the warning. The warning is:

```
[W Resize.cpp:24] Warning: An output with one or more elements was resized since it had shape [1, 16, 16], which does not match the required output shape [1, 1, 16, 16]. This behavior is deprecated, and in a future PyTorch release outputs will not be resized unless they have zero elements. You can explicitly reuse an out tensor t by resizing it, inplace, to zero elements with t.resize_(0). (function resize_output_check)
```

(my inputs are 16x16 tensors).  Note: despite the warning, the calculated matrix exponential *is* still correct (when compared with the output of expm::expm() applied to the corresponding matrix (non-tensor).  I'm using torch 0.9.1 under R 4.2.2.

Code to replicate the problem:

```

aa <- torch_tensor(a)
b <- a * 1e-3
bb <- torch_tensor(b)

title: 'glue' should be an import
description: 'glue' should be under 'imports' rather than 'suggests' as it is a hard dependency (used in conditions.R and distributions-constraints.R). Currently installing 'torch' does not automatically install 'glue' and it will proceed to error with package not found.

title: Release torch 0.9.1
description:
Prepare for release:

* [x] `rhub::check_with_sanitizers()`
* [x] `revdepcheck::cloud_check()`
* [x] Update `cran-comments.md`
* [x] `git push`
* [x] Create the cran/ branch and update the branch variable

title: torch_manual_seed does not seem to work with $sample()
description:
Hi,

This is my first time writing on GitHub, so I am unsure if I have included everything you need.

I have a question regarding reproducibility when generating random numbers from distributions.
From pages 36 and 37 in the manual (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/torch/torch.pdf) it seems that I should use the $sample() function, but then I am not able to set the seed and reproduce the sampled values even when setting the seed.
However,  setting the seed works when I use $rsample(). Is there a particular reason for this?

P.S.  I think you have done a splendid job in making torch much more available for us R users!


```R
library(torch)
dn = distr_normal(0, 1)

# These calls do NOT generate the same value
torch_manual_seed(10)
dn$sample(1)
torch_manual_seed(10)
dn$sample(1)

# These calls do NOT generate the same value (checking if I needed to set seed both in R and torch)
torch_manual_seed(10)
set.seed(10)
dn$sample(1)
torch_manual_seed(10)
set.seed(10)
dn$sample(1)

# These calls do generate the same value
torch_manual_seed(10)
dn$rsample(1)
torch_manual_seed(10)
dn$rsample(1)
```

title: [feature request] Way to load state dict for corrup model (invalid external pointers)
description:
Hey, thank you very much for taking the time!

I have some questions regarding the serialization of torch models. 
In mlr3torch we have learners (R6 classes) that have a field `$model` in which the network (the actual network, not the module), the optimizer and the loss function are saved. This means that after saving and loading via `saveRDS` and `readRDS` the torch tensors can be broken. This is problematic for parallelization using `future.apply` so I have to address this somehow. 

What I want to do is the following: 
1. Give the learner a method `$serialize()` that converts the torch tensors to raws (using the function               `torch:::tensor_to_raw_vector_with_class`. These are then simply stored in the learner and allow to fully store the learners information in a rds file. 
2. Give the learner a method `$unserialize()` which converts the R raws to torch tensors and then loads it as the state dict of the network, optimizer and loss function

However I stumled across some problems: 

1. The functions that I am using are currently not exported (like `tensor_to_raw_vector_with_class`) 
2. One cannot simply call `$load_state_dict()` on a corrupt `nn_module()`, meaning a nn_module whose parameters and buffers are invalid pointers. 

Is it possible to export those functions and provide a function to load a state dict for a nn_module with corrupt tensors / does this even make sense? 

I would be willing to make a PR as well if you think this makes sense and is relatively easy to implement :)

Cheers, 

Sebastian

title: Is it possible to detect if tensor is sparse or dense?
description:
I'm trying to make a custom collate_fn where some of my data is sparse and some dense. With the sparse data I want to stack and then use to_dense() but with the dense I only want to stack.

In pytorch there is the function [is_sparse](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/1022443168b5fad55bbd03d087abf574c9d2e9df/torch/_linalg_utils.py#L11) which relies on the tensor.layout property. 

It doesn't seem like the layout property is exposed here. Is it possible to expose it so I can detect if the tensor is sparse? Or is there already some way to do it?

Regards,
Egill

title: torch_bernoulli() is failing on device="cuda" with Error :    Expected a 'cuda' device type for generator but found 'cpu'
description:
Hello,

`torch_bernoulli()` distribution is failing on CUDA device with the following error message
```
Error in (function (self, generator)  : 
  Expected a 'cuda' device type for generator but found 'cpu'
```
whereas it is working as expected on CPU device.


## Workaround

Even if it is non-sense with regards to performance, a workaround is to compute the bernoulli in CPU before moving the result to GPU :
```  r
library(torch)
cuda_is_available()
#> [1] TRUE
# workaround
torch_bernoulli(torch_ones(3,3, device="cpu") * 0.5)$to(device="cuda")
#> torch_tensor
#>  1  0  1
#>  0  0  1
#>  0  1  0
#> [ CUDAFloatType{3,3} ]
```

## Reprex
``` r
library(torch)
cuda_is_available()
#> [1] TRUE
# working function on device="cpu"
torch_bernoulli(torch_ones(3,3, device="cpu") * 0.5)
#> torch_tensor
#>  1  0  0
#>  0  1  0
#>  0  1  1
#> [ CPUFloatType{3,3} ]
# failing function on device = "cuda"
torch_bernoulli(torch_ones(3,3, device="cuda")* 0.5)

title: `$movedim()` parameters source and destination are 0-indexed even if `torch_movedim()` ones are 1-indexed
description:
# Current behavour
`$movedim()`  use 0-indexed dimensions for its parameters source and destination. This is not expected, create a lot of confusion is the {torch} perfect world where everything is 1-indexed:
```r
t <- torch_randn(c(3,2,1))
t$movedim(0,1)
#> torch_tensor
#> (1,.,.) = 
#>  -0.4625
#>   1.0214
#>   1.1491
#> 
#> (2,.,.) = 
#>  -1.1606
#>  -0.5315
#>   0.4522
#> [ CPUFloatType{2,3,1} ]
```

For information, `torch_movedim()`source and destination are correctly 1-indexed 

# Expected behavor
`$movedim()`  source and destination should be 1-indexed dimensions.

# ReprEx
``` r
library(torch)
library(testthat)
t <- torch_randn(c(3,2,1))

# this is the expected behavior
expect_equal(t$movedim(1,2)$shape, torch_movedim(t, 1, 2)$shape)
#> Error: t$movedim(1, 2)$shape not equal to torch_movedim(t, 1, 2)$shape.
#> 3/3 mismatches (average diff: 1.33)
#> [1] 3 - 2 ==  1
#> [2] 1 - 3 == -2
#> [3] 2 - 1 ==  1

# the following is unexpected
expect_equal(t$movedim(0,1)$shape, torch_movedim(t, 1, 2)$shape)
```

title: torch_tile not working as expected
description:
`torch_tile()` seems to be expecting its `dim` argument to follow R dimension numbering convention (1, 2, ...) and subtracts 1 before passing on the call - but dim here really stands for number of repetitions per dimension:


```
> t <- torch_tensor(rbind(c(1, 2), c(3,4)))
> t$tile(c(2, 2))
torch_tensor
 1  2
 3  4
[ CPUFloatType{2,2} ]
> t$tile(c(3, 3))
torch_tensor
 1  2  1  2
 3  4  3  4
 1  2  1  2
 3  4  3  4
[ CPUFloatType{4,4} ]
```

compare https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.tile.html#torch.tile:

```
>>> y = torch.tensor([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
>>> torch.tile(y, (2, 2))
tensor([[1, 2, 1, 2],
        [3, 4, 3, 4],
        [1, 2, 1, 2],
        [3, 4, 3, 4]])


```

For my Transformer model I get peak GPU memory of 3.2 GiB as well in R but in pytorch 839MiB

This is quite a lot of difference, 3-4x. 

Any idea what could be the cause?

title: torch_bincount is 0 indexed
description:
Hello, torch has been great so far in R and I have found it to be really helpful. Just a small possible bug I found.

It looks like the torch_bincount function gives incorrect results if underlying data is 1-indexed. For example, the vector `c(1,1,2,2,8)` will give

```
torch_tensor(as.integer(c(1,1,2,2,8)))$bincount()
#torch_tensor
# 0
# 2
# 2
# 0
# 0
# 0
# 0
# 0
# 1
# [ CPULongType{9} ]
```
which is length 9. I would expect this function to look more like the results from R's `table` function:
```
table(c(1,1,2,2,8))
#1 2 8 
#2 2 1 
```


If we subtract one from the index, we get,
```
torch_tensor(as.integer(c(1,1,2,2,8)-1))$bincount()
torch_tensor
# 2
# 2
# 0
# 0
# 0
# 0
# 0
# 1
#[ CPULongType{8} ]
```
which is the result I would have expected. Not sure if this is expected behavior.

A proposed change to the `torch_bincount` function would be to add an extra line that changes the R index to a C index:
```
function (self, weights = list(), minlength = 0L) 
{
  args <- mget(x = c("self", "weights", "minlength"))
  args$self <- torch_sub(args$self, 1L)
  expected_types <- list(self = "Tensor", weights = "Tensor", 
                         minlength = "int64_t")
  nd_args <- "self"
  return_types <- list(list("Tensor"))
  call_c_function(fun_name = "bincount", args = args, expected_types = expected_types, 
                  nd_args = nd_args, return_types = return_types, fun_type = "namespace")
}
```

                              layout = torch_strided(), device = NULL,
                              requires_grad = FALSE) {
  if (is.null(dtype)) {
    dtype <- torch_float()
  }

  opt <- torch_tensor_options(
    dtype = dtype, layout = layout, device = device,
    requires_grad = requires_grad
  )

  if (is.null(window_length)) {
    value_error("argument 'window_length' must be int, not NULL")
  }

  .torch_hann_window(
    window_length = window_length, periodic = periodic,
    options = opt
  )
}


```

title: methods not implemented for 'Half'  - `torch_float16()`
description:
Hello,

# Current situation

I'm trying to reduce the memory footprint of my nn_modules through `torch_float16()` tensors. But a lot of methods raise a
```log
`object` threw an unexpected error.
Message: "LayerNormKernelImpl" not implemented for 'Half'
Exception raised from operator() at /pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/layer_norm_kernel.cpp:90 (most recent call first):
```
I've been able to spot the following torch functions having the issue (not an exhaustive list )
```r
nn_linear()
nn_softmax()
nn_layer_norm()
```

# Workaround

It is possible to switch the tensor to toch_float32() before and back to torch_float16() after any of those functions, but it is a coding nightmare, kills code readability, and do not reach the goal of reducing the memory and compute footprint.

title: R crash
description:
This is probably not the finest nor precise question... but here we go. 

In some applications we are bootstrapping a torch-based model (nothing too fancy, mostly some variant of a fully-connected net), so basically estimating it many times (typically <100). On most computers, R ends ups crashing/freezing at some point for some bootstrap. Something even the whole computer crashes. The bootstrap for which it fails is random, sometimes it after 3 runs, sometimes after 60, but it always crashes if we consider enough runs. Quite interestingly, we have noticed this never occurs on M1 Macs of any kind, and neither on Colab.  However, it fails on other macs and the universe of PCs we tried.   

If there are any insights on what might be going on, we'll gladly take it -- as this is a substantial obstacle to use sharing our torch-based code in R.

title: Fail Gracefully with NULL tensors
description:
NULLs passed to torch_tensor fail gracefully.
``` r
torch::torch_tensor(NULL)
#> Error in torch_tensor_cpp(data, dtype, device, requires_grad, pin_memory): R type not handled
```

NULLs passed to torch_tensor as integers "work".
```r
torch::torch_tensor(as.integer(NULL))
#> torch_tensor
#> [ CPULongType{0} ]
```

But if you subset that tensor, it causes R to crash.
```r
# Crashes Rstudio.
torch::torch_tensor(as.integer(NULL))[1]
```

This can happen relatively easily with a malformed dataset (for example, if you try to construct labels in a test set), and the crash is mysterious.

Should `torch_tensor` validate the `data` argument to give a friendlier error message for (any type of) NULL?

title: bug in weight decay for adam optimizer
description:
I found a typo in the adam optimizer loop_fun [here](https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/main/R/optim-adam.R#L96)

It is:

```R  
grad$add_(p, alpha = group$weight_decay) 
```

But should be:

```R  
grad$add_(param, alpha = group$weight_decay) 
```
I was comparing the same models in pytorch and torch and found that there were some differences. After a lot of debugging where I tried to overfit one random batch and removed more and more parts of my code I finally identified the weight decay in Adam to be the culprit. With a deep-ish resnet of 8 layers and some weight decay I couldn't overfit one batch, while pytorch did it easily for the same model.

I was going to add a quick pull request to fix it but I'm a bit stuck on how to write a test to catch this..

title: libtorch_cpu.so replaces some of R's built-in lapack routines
description:
I have been working on a problem which I am having a very hard time to reproduce consistently. If I run the code that we have just as it is, I get 8 out of 12 threads spawned by mclapply to simply stop responding, using 0% CPU. To debug this I started to add ```cat``` statements all over the code, and eventually narrowed it down to the R function ```chol2inv```.

Here begins the interesting part. I had no problems with the exact same setup before adding torch as a dependency to the package that I am developing. When torch is loaded, the problems seem to start. I then went on to make R print the pid of each thread so that I could determine which threads were the problematic ones. Attaching gdb to one of the problematic threads gave me some interesting information:

```
(gdb) where
#0  0x00007fe4e6522113 in ?? () from /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1
#1  0x00007fe4e6520dd9 in ?? () from /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1
#2  0x00007fe4c70ada93 in mkl_blas_dtrmm () from /home/jon/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/3.6/torch/deps/./libtorch_cpu.so
#3  0x00007fe4c707a27b in mkl_lapack_dtrtri () from /home/jon/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/3.6/torch/deps/./libtorch_cpu.so
#4  0x00007fe4bff10b66 in mkl_lapack_dpotri () from /home/jon/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/3.6/torch/deps/./libtorch_cpu.so
#5  0x00007fe4bfd0f280 in mkl_lapack.dpotri_ () from /home/jon/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/3.6/torch/deps/./libtorch_cpu.so
#6  0x00007fe4ba53a11b in ?? () from /usr/lib/R/modules//lapack.so
#7  0x00007fe4ba53b74e in ?? () from /usr/lib/R/modules//lapack.so
#8  0x00007fe4e89d4ed1 in ?? () from /usr/lib/R/lib/libR.so
#9  0x00007fe4e89e1c80 in Rf_eval () from /usr/lib/R/lib/libR.so
```

We can see that the call to ```chol2inv``` ended up inside a lapack routine from libtorch_cpu.so. It seems that the problem then is that we encounter a strange edge case where my multithreading from mclapply causes something to break inside ```dpotri```, when it itself tries to multithread.

I have tried to create a minimal example to reproduce this, with limited success. I am unable to share the code that causes the problem as it is proprietary. Sorry for this.

Do you have any input on the situation? Is this expected behaviour that torch should replace the internal functions? Is it possible to have them co-exist peacefully?

title: Modifying dataloader sampler after creation
description:
Hi @dfalbel,

Is there a relatively safe way to modify a `dataloader()` after it has been instantiated? For example, let's say a dataloader is created with `shuffle = TRUE` (and thus `torch:::RandomSampler` is used instead of `torch:::SequentialSampler`), is a brute-force change of this sampler "safe"?

For example:
``` r
library(torch)

ds <- 
  dataset(
    initialize = function(n) {
      self$x <- 
        torch_tensor(matrix(rnorm(n * 100), nrow = n))
      self$y <- 
        torch_tensor(matrix(sample(0:1, n, TRUE), nrow = n))$to(torch_float())
    },
    .length = function() {
      dim(self$x)[[1]]
    },
    .getitem = function(i) {
      list(
        self$x[i, ],
        self$y[i]
      )
    }
  )

train_dl <- dataloader(ds(2000), batch_size = 32, shuffle = TRUE)

train_dl$sampler
#> <utils_sampler_random>
#>   Inherits from: <utils_sampler>
#>   Public:
#>     .iter: function () 
#>     .length: function () 
#>     .num_samples: NULL
#>     clone: function (deep = FALSE) 
#>     data_source: dataset, R6
#>     generator: NULL
#>     initialize: function (data_source, replacement = FALSE, num_samples = NULL, 
#>     num_samples: active binding
#>     replacement: FALSE

train_dl$sampler <- torch:::SequentialSampler

train_dl$sampler
#> <utils_sampler_sequential> object generator
#>   Inherits from: <Sampler>
#>   Public:
#>     initialize: function (data_source) 
#>     .iter: function () 
#>     .length: function () 
#>     clone: function (deep = FALSE) 
#>   Parent env: <environment: namespace:torch>
#>   Locked objects: FALSE
#>   Locked class: FALSE
#>   Portable: TRUE
```

Obviously using non-namespaced objects (i.e. `torch:::`) is generally not advisable, but is this kind of brute-force change destructive to the dataloader in any way? Does the batch sampler need to be re-initialized too?

Related, I was thinking that perhaps the `shuffle` argument should be contained in the dataloader object as an active binding that queries the `sampler`. What do you think? Something like:
```r
DataLoader <- R6::R6Class(
  classname = "dataloader",
  lock_objects = FALSE,
  ...
  active = list(
    shuffle = function() {
      # code to check if Sequential or Random sampler...
    }
  )
```
In fact, if the `shuffle` active binding accepted a single argument, it could perhaps be used to address the original question about safely changing from a random or sequential dataloader _post-hoc_.
```r
train_dl <- dataloader(ds(2000), batch_size = 32, shuffle = TRUE)
train_dl$shuffle <- FALSE # does internal changes to make sequential
```

Thoughts? Sorry for the long issue...

title: Reorganizing the docs
description:
I was looking at more places to help improve the torch docs (all of https://torch.mlverse.org/), and I think by far the most useful thing would be to clean up the organization of the docs. Right now there is lots of content spread all over, and the important stuff isn't necessarily highest in the hierarchy. Today, the page is split up like this:

* Homepage - details of the other packages
* Get started - set of three tutorials
* Get technical - more examples
* Use torch - a five part tutorial
* Resources - links to external things that could be useful
* Docs
  * Articles - details of using torch based on vignettes
  * Examples - some sparse examples
  * Reference - extremely useful and important list of all functions
  * Changelog

I think there are a few issues with this layout, including:

1. "examples" meaning things that are just code you can run, documented single examples, and full on tutorials are split into multiple places. It's not clear why some examples are in one place and not others, and it's not clear what a person should start with
2. some really important content that most users care about, like the reference, is nested deeply and not easy to find
3. There isn't a clear "here is the first page you should read to do a hello, word torch model"
3. For reasons I assume are due to using packagedown, the navbar changes depending on if you're on the /docs page, which makes it hard to navigate.

---

I think it would be a good idea to rearrange the pages a bit (even if it means changing where things live on the backend for packagedown reasons), into something like the following:

* Homepage - the exact same as today
* Examples
  * Quickstart - new, a single example that just shows using torch in a few lines
  * Full torch tutorial - what is currently called "use torch"
  * Examples by topic - these are what is currently called "get technical"
* Articles - the same as the existing articles section
* Reference - the same as the existing reference
* Get help
  * External resources - same as the existing resources page, including a link to torch-learnr
  * Contact - links for how to make requests (probably github and stack overflow)
  * Changelog - same as today

Removed from the website would be:
* https://torch.mlverse.org/start/ - the three tutorials listed here would get merged into other pages, like the dataloader one
* https://torch.mlverse.org/docs/articles/examples - these examples are pretty empty and I think the other examples do a better job

The benefits of this layout are

1. Now things are coalesced--the examples are all in one area for instance
2. All the important stuff can be seen from a consistent top navbar
3. It should be easier for new users to understand where to go (probably "quickstart")

---

I am happy to take on doing this docs reorg! My questions are (1) would y'all be okay with this broadly? (2) do you have thoughts on the particular layout I proposed? This is somewhat similar to what we did for the [Saturn Cloud docs](http://saturncloud.io/docs) and I've been pretty happy with it.

title: Guidelines on how to combine mclapply and torch
description:
Hi! I am just learning to use pytorch through this library. So far I really appreciate the effort that has gone into it and how easy it is to port code from python to R.

I am however missing one thing in the documentation. I have a use case where I want to use torch inside a thread spawned (or forked rather) by mclapply. My experience so far has been varied on OSX and Ubuntu. 

On OSX it works "some of the time", and some of the time I get the long error with the comment:
```Unable to handle autograd's threading in combination with fork-based multiprocessing.```
However, when I do not get this error, everything works fine and only one thread per mclapply thread appears to be running (looking in htop for example). The code also runs at a reasonable speed.

On Ubuntu (running virtually on the same computer) As many threads as there are threads available on the CPU are allocated, and it is running roughly 10x slower than on OSX. I am able to solve this by a call to torch_set_num_threads(1) just before the other torch code in each mclapply thread.

My question is; what are the recommendations for running torch inside mclapply (if it is even advisable)? Is it possible to add some documentation for this to make it easier for the next person encountering the same problem?

Please let me know if you need me to extract some examples from the codebase that I am working on.

title: Issues in manual implementation of the optimization process for ODE parameters
description:
Recently I was trying to implement the ODE parameter optimization using autograd function in torch. The data were simulated using the ODEs below (a 2-compartment pharmacokinetic model, in ODE form rather than solved/explicit form):

da1/dt=-cl/v1 * amt1-cld/v1 * amt1+cld/v2 * amt2
da2/dt=cld/v1 * amt1-cld/v2 * amt2

observation(cc) = a1/v1, with additive error ~ 5; a1(0) = 1200000, a2(0) = 0, cl=100, cld=200, v1=3000, v2=5000.

The simulated observations are as follows.

time | cc
-- | --
4 | 275.2478
8 | 196.7948
12 | 153.0787
24 | 89.82291
36 | 72.17694
48 | 61.54845
72 | 45.67833
96 | 39.92614
120 | 25.65196
144 | 23.36927
168 | 17.25322

And I tried to build the loss function using RK4 solver, with the R code below:

```
grad_amt1<-function(amt1,amt2,theta_cl,theta_v1,theta_v2,theta_cld){
  da1dt=-theta_cl/theta_v1 * amt1-theta_cld/theta_v1 * amt1+theta_cld/theta_v2 * amt2
  return(da1dt)
}

grad_amt2<-function(amt1,amt2,theta_cl,theta_v1,theta_v2,theta_cld){
  da2dt=theta_cld/theta_v1 * amt1-theta_cld/theta_v2 * amt2
  return(da2dt)
}

runge_kutta<-function(dose){
  
  a1<-dose
  a2<-0
  time_step<-4
  t<-0
  j<-1
  ofv<-0
  
  while(t<168){
  
  k1_amt1<-grad_amt1(a1,a2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
  k1_amt2<-grad_amt2(a1,a2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
  
  k2_amt1<-grad_amt1(a1+time_step/2 * k1_amt1,a2+time_step/2 * k1_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
  k2_amt2<-grad_amt2(a1+time_step/2 * k1_amt1,a2+time_step/2 * k1_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
  
  k3_amt1<-grad_amt1(a1+time_step/2 * k2_amt1,a2+time_step/2 * k2_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
  k3_amt2<-grad_amt2(a1+time_step/2 * k2_amt1,a2+time_step/2 * k2_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
  
  k4_amt1<-grad_amt1(a1+time_step * k3_amt1,a2+time_step * k3_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
  k4_amt2<-grad_amt2(a1+time_step * k3_amt1,a2+time_step * k3_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
  
  slp_amt1<-(k1_amt1+2 * k2_amt1+2 * k3_amt1+k4_amt1)/6
  slp_amt2<-(k1_amt2+2 * k2_amt2+2 * k3_amt2+k4_amt2)/6
  
  a1<-a1+slp_amt1 * time_step
  a2<-a2+slp_amt2 * time_step
  
  t<-t+time_step
  
  for (i in j:nrow(dat))
    if (dat[i,"time"]==t){
      ofv<-ofv+(dat[i,"cc"]-a1/v1)^2
      j<-j+1
      break}
  }
  
  return(ofv)
}
```

Then I tried to obtain the gradient of the loss function (ofv) to those 4 parameters (cl,v1,v2,cld) using autograd, and optimize using steepest descent approach (but not Newton or Nelder-Mead approach):

```
cl <- torch_tensor(c(80),requires_grad=TRUE)
v1 <- torch_tensor(c(2000),requires_grad=TRUE)
v2 <- torch_tensor(c(4000),requires_grad=TRUE)
cld <- torch_tensor(c(100),requires_grad=TRUE)
rate<-0.1

for (x in 1:10){
  loss_function<-runge_kutta(1200000)
  loss_function$backward()

  with_no_grad({

  cl$sub_(rate * cl$grad)
  v1$sub_(rate * v1$grad)
  v2$sub_(rate * v2$grad)
  cld$sub_(rate * cld$grad)
  
  cl$grad$zero_()
  v1$grad$zero_()
  v2$grad$zero_()
  cld$grad$zero_()

  })
  
  OBJFV<-runge_kutta(1200000)
  print(paste("Objective function value = ",as.numeric(OBJFV),sep=""))
}
```

However, according to my observation the grad for v1 and v2 is very small (~0), thus these 2 parameters cannot be updated even with large step. At the same time, when I use built-in function optim or nlm in R (for both gradient dependent or gradient-free approach), it can give unbiased estimation:

```
runge_kutta<-function(x){
  
  cl<-x[1]
  v1<-x[2]
  v2<-x[3]
  cld<-x[4]
  
  a1<-1200000
  a2<-0
  time_step<-4
  t<-0
  j<-1
  ofv<-0
  
  while(t<168){
    
    k1_amt1<-grad_amt1(a1,a2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
    k1_amt2<-grad_amt2(a1,a2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
    
    k2_amt1<-grad_amt1(a1+time_step/2 * k1_amt1,a2+time_step/2 * k1_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
    k2_amt2<-grad_amt2(a1+time_step/2 * k1_amt1,a2+time_step/2 * k1_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
    
    k3_amt1<-grad_amt1(a1+time_step/2 * k2_amt1,a2+time_step/2 * k2_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
    k3_amt2<-grad_amt2(a1+time_step/2 * k2_amt1,a2+time_step/2 * k2_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
    
    k4_amt1<-grad_amt1(a1+time_step * k3_amt1,a2+time_step * k3_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
    k4_amt2<-grad_amt2(a1+time_step * k3_amt1,a2+time_step * k3_amt2,cl,v1,v2,cld)
    
    slp_amt1<-(k1_amt1+2 * k2_amt1+2 * k3_amt1+k4_amt1)/6
    slp_amt2<-(k1_amt2+2 * k2_amt2+2 * k3_amt2+k4_amt2)/6
    
    a1<-a1+slp_amt1 * time_step
    a2<-a2+slp_amt2 * time_step
    
    t<-t+time_step
    
    for (i in j:nrow(dat))
      if (dat[i,"time"]==t){
        ofv<-ofv+(dat[i,"cc"]-a1/v1)^2
        j<-j+1
        break}
  }
  
  ofv
}

optim(par=c(10,2000,2000,10),fn=runge_kutta,method="Nelder-Mead",hessian = TRUE)

nlm(runge_kutta,c(10,2000,2000,10),hessian = TRUE)
```

Then there must be something wrong with my first approah using torch. Could someone help me?

title: Torch barely utilizes GPU
description:
Hi!

I recently ported a simple demo model from R TensorFlow to R Torch (both with the GPU). I was surprised that the Torch model seems to be dramatically slower than the TensorFlow one (like 10x slower), and when using the command `watch nvidia-smi` it looks like Torch is only using 1% of the attached GPU. I'm not sure where the issue lies, nor where I would reach out to help for figuring it out. Do you all have suggestions for debugging GPU issues with the package, or could point me in the right direction? Thanks!

_**Picture of the GPU barely being utilized by Torch**_

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3317138/152881319-aa0d60ab-03ab-4014-8c88-28d08089b636.png)


_**Working example of the code**_

```r
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)
library(torch)
library(glue)
library(progress)

device <- torch_device("cuda")

character_lookup <- data.frame(character = c(letters,".","-"," ","+"))
character_lookup[["character_id"]] <- as.integer(1:nrow(character_lookup))
max_length <- 10
num_characters <- nrow(character_lookup) + 1

text_matrix <- read_rds("https://saturn-public-data.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/pet-names/pet-data-matrix.rds")

data_x <- 
  (text_matrix + 1L) %>%
  torch_tensor(device = device) %>%
  {{.[,1:max_length]}} %>%
  nnf_one_hot(num_characters+1) %>%
  {{.$to(dtype= torch_float())}}

data_y <- 
  text_matrix[,max_length+1] %>%
  torch_tensor(device = device)

pet_dataset <- dataset(
  name = "pet_dataset",
  initialize = function(){
    self$data_x <- data_x
    self$data_y <- data_y
  },
  .getitem = function(index){
    x <- self$data_x[index,,]
    y <- self$data_y[index]
    list(x, y)
  },
  .length = function() {
    self$data_y$size()[[1]]
  }
)

network <- nn_module(
  "PetNameNetwork",
  initialize = function() {
    self$num_layers <- 2
    self$hidden_size <- 32
    self$lstm <- torch::nn_lstm(
      input_size = num_characters+1,
      hidden_size = self$hidden_size,
      num_layers = self$num_layers,
      batch_first = TRUE,
      dropout = 0.1
    )
    self$fc = nn_linear(self$hidden_size, num_characters)
  },
  forward = function(x){
    result <- self$lstm(x)
    hidden <- result[[2]][[2]]
    self$fc(hidden[self$num_layers,])
  }
)

batch_size <- 1024
num_epochs <- 25
data <- pet_dataset()
data_loader <- dataloader(data, batch_size = batch_size)
model <- network()$to(device = device)
optimizer <- optim_adam(model$parameters)
criterion <- nn_cross_entropy_loss()

for(epoch_num in 1:num_epochs){
  pb <- progress::progress_bar$new(
    total = ceiling(data$.length()/batch_size),
    format = glue("[:bar] Epoch {epoch_num} :percent eta: :eta")
  )
  coro::loop( for (batch in data_loader){
    optimizer$zero_grad()
    output <- model(batch[[1]])
    loss <- criterion(output, batch[[2]])
    loss$backward()
    optimizer$step()
    pb$tick()
  })
  message(glue("{Sys.time()} - epoch {epoch_num}/",
               "{num_epochs} complete - loss {loss$item()}"))
}
```

title: Feature request: torch.nn.Flatten() equivalent module for nn_sequential
description:
I wanted to transfer the PyTorch Basics examples to R torch. 
https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/pytorch_with_examples.html#nn-module
within there:
```
model = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Linear(3, 1),
    torch.nn.Flatten(0, 1)
)
```
I am not able to find an equivalent `nn_flatten` module in the R `torch` library. 
According to https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53953460/how-to-flatten-input-in-nn-sequential-in-pytorch  
`torch.nn.Flatten()` could be implemented within PyTorch as an own class, eg:   
```
class Flatten(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        batch_size = x.shape[0]
        return x.view(batch_size, -1)
 ```
at former times, when `torch.nn.Flatten()` did not exist there.
Could this be done in R `torch` as well? If so how?

    print("exp2 forward..")
    result <- i$exp()
    ctx$save_for_backward(result = result)

)

title: Implementing MMD-VAE in torch, need specific functions (e.g. torch_tile)
description:
Thanks a lot for your great work!

I need to implement an MMD Variational Autoencoder (https://ermongroup.github.io/blog/a-tutorial-on-mmd-variational-autoencoders/) in ```torch```, but I am having some issues translating the following functions from ```keras``` to ```torch```.

```
source: https://keras.rstudio.com/articles/examples/mmd_cvae.html

compute_kernel <- function(x, y) {
  x_size <- k_shape(x)[1]
  y_size <- k_shape(y)[1]
  dim <- k_shape(x)[2]
  tiled_x <- k_tile(k_reshape(x, k_stack(list(x_size, 1, dim))), k_stack(list(1, y_size, 1)))
  tiled_y <- k_tile(k_reshape(y, k_stack(list(1, y_size, dim))), k_stack(list(x_size, 1, 1)))
  k_exp(-k_mean(k_square(tiled_x - tiled_y), axis = 3) / k_cast(dim, tf$float64))
}

compute_mmd <- function(x, y, sigma_sqr = 1) {
  x_kernel <- compute_kernel(x, x)
  y_kernel <- compute_kernel(y, y)
  xy_kernel <- compute_kernel(x, y)
  k_mean(x_kernel) + k_mean(y_kernel) - 2 * k_mean(xy_kernel)
}
```

Specifically, to re-implement the functions above, I was hoping to get some help finding the ```torch``` equivalents of ```keras``` ```k_shape``` and ```k_tile``` for Tensor manipulation. I already found ```torch_stack``` and ```torch_reshape```, which seem to be the same as ```k_stack``` and ```k_reshape```, and I am guessing ```torch_float64``` can replace ```k_cast``` above but I am not sure.

Any help would be much appreciated.

title: An idea: a function to retrieve unexported `torch_` prefixed functions? (because I need one of them)
description:
I just want to start this (long) issue by saying what an incredible package this is and what a resource to the R / machine learning / statistical inference community! I have been studying the package design over the last few months and have frequently been amazed at what a fascinating build system it is.

In the process of studying this package and also trying to port some complicated Pytorch code I have noted that there is a large number of autogenerated R functions that interface with underlying `libtorch` c++ functions. These are all prefixed with `torch_` and many are not exported (by design presumably, as they are mostly meant to be used in other exported functions). However, currently many of these functions are actually totally unused anywhere in any exported function. This made me wonder if there would be value in a function designed specifically for advanced users that allowed access to these functions, without having to export them all and clutter the public namespace? So something along the lines of an `call_torch_function(func_name, args)`, which would construct a call to the unexported function and return the result. Warnings would have to be made to users that you would really have to know what you are doing to use this (and it is at your own risk), since all the functions have not been wrapped in an R-friendly way (e.g. changing indexing to 1-based instead of 0-based, etc.), and many also are presumably untested (?).

I have a particular use-case in mind. In the Pytorch project I am porting they use a call directly to an operation `cudnn_convolution_backward_weight`. After digging around for awhile I discovered `torch:::torch_cudnn_convolution_backward_weight()` exists as an unexported function in `torch` (with the same function signature). Now, I realise I could request this function be exported, but then it would kind of hang there by itself in the package, as something hardly anyone would use. And then the question is, should also `torch::torch_cudnn_convolution_backward_input()` be exported for consistency? What about all the other `cudnn_convolution_` operations? These functions are potentially useful, but only in limited circumstances, and usually only by very advanced users. That is why I think a function that could send a call to any of these might make sense. Note that I am not thinking it should allow access to any non-exported function in the package, just the `torch_` prefixed ones, since these are all in `Declarations.yaml`, which could be the criteria for allowing access to advanced users (or `torch` developers if you prefer). A function like this would also allow R package developers to write their own user friendly wrappers for `libtorch` functions that are currently unwrapped in `torch` itself.

Anyway, just a (possibly crazy) thought. Feel free to shoot it down immediately. In that case though, can I get that `torch_cudnn_convolution_backward_weight()` function exported? Happy to make a PR for it (or for the above idea). Thanks again for the great package.

title: Adding new `torch` extensions to `contrib`.
description:
I've been slowly working my way through a port of a big Pytorch project to R `torch` (StyleGAN3: https://github.com/NVlabs/stylegan3). I've managed to make my way about half way through the Generator architecture, but now I need some Pytorch extensions used in the Stylegan3 repository. These include custom CUDA code (everything can be found here: https://github.com/NVlabs/stylegan3/tree/main/torch_utils/ops). By following this PR: https://github.com/mlverse/torch/pull/619, I was able to get one of the extensions working on a fork of the `torch` repo (the `bias_act` extension). But before I go ahead and expend energy on getting the other extensions to work, I just wanted to make sure it was okay to continue with this approach? This will require making a PR of these added extensions (which I am putting in the `contrib` section), and so I wanted to make sure you were okay with this contribution? There are two things to consider:

1) The extensions take quite awhile to compile, and so add an appreciable amount to the compilation time of `lantern`.
2) Is the license for these extensions acceptable for the `torch` project? The license can be found here: https://github.com/NVlabs/stylegan3/blob/main/LICENSE.txt . It is copyrighted by NVIDIA but it does grant the right to redistribution and modification, though use of the code is restricted to non-commercial purposes. A warning to users about this restriction could be included in the function documentation for functions using this contributed code. What do you think?

Alternatively, various hints around this repo suggest that there may soon be ways of adding extensions without having to add them to `torch` itself, but instead through a mechanism in a separate package. Am I correct that this functionality may be on the way, and if show, do you think I should wait for it? Obviously it would be nice (for me) to use the compilation infrastructure already setup for `torch`, but I'm interested in whatever options might be (or become) available.

Thanks very much for your time. (In case you are interested, early work on this project is here: https://github.com/rdinnager/styleganr).

title: Torch decrements the index by one
description:
Hello, I have discovered an error (at least from my point of view) in the indexing of torch tensors with R vectors:
```{r}
library(torch)
torch_manual_seed(1234)

i <- c(2, 4)
a <- torch_randn(5, 5)

# Indexing tensor a
result <- a[, i]

# But the index has changed
i
#> [1] 1 3
```
I assume this behavior is not intended, right?

**Note:** This problem only exists when `i` is a normal R vector. If `i` is a torch object instead, everything runs as you would expect.

```
nn2 <- nn_module(classname = "hello", inherit = nn_linear)

title: torch_ne(): output is not interpretable as logical
description:
Hi.

Below example shows that `torch_equal()` can be used in an `if` statement, but this is not the case for `torch_ne(), torch_greater(), torch_greater_equal(), torch_less()` and `torch_less_equal()`. Reproducible example below: 

```
x <- torch_tensor(1L)
y <- torch_tensor(1L)

if(torch_equal(x, y)){
  print("in torch_equal")
}
# NO ERROR

x <- torch_tensor(1L)
y <- torch_tensor(2L)

if(torch_ne(x, y)){
  print("in torch_ne")
}

# Error in if (torch_ne(x, y)) { : argument is not interpretable as logical

torch_greater(x, y)
torch_greater_equal(x, y)
torch_less(x, y)
torch_less_equal(x, y)
# Error in if (torch_ne(x, y)) { : argument is not interpretable as logical
```
Note that Python `torch.ne` gives a `True/False` output that can be used in` if `statements. 
[https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.ne.html](url)
```
torch.ne(torch.tensor(1), torch.tensor(2))
tensor(True)
```
I imagine these logical statements would be most useful in `if `statements but Torch give error for this use.

title: Debugging backward() with register_hook(). And new solution?
description:
Hi,

Whilst debugging issue #634, I've been using register_hook() for the autograd's backward pass. I'm getting this error message. 

```
Error in (function (tensors, dim)  : 
  CUDA error: device-side assert triggered
CUDA kernel errors might be asynchronously reported at some other API call,so the stacktrace below might be incorrect. For debugging consider passing CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1.
```
 
The pytorch advice for this error message is to run `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 python script.py` , but I don't know what an R equivalent is for passing `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`?

In order to understand register_hook() I produced the below code, which gave me a thought (potential solution) for debugging autograd's backward pass. Why can't a tensor object have a functionality called Tensor$Browser (TRUE/FALSE) and when set as TRUE it executes a browser() during loss$backward() for all tensors with `grad_fn`.  

Tensor$browser would behave just like in the below functions (c_hook, d_hook and e_hook) but you can activate the browsers when calling loss$backward(Browser = TRUE) . title: with_detect_anomaly provides "unknown line number" in  traceback()
description:
Hi, 

Below addresses bug with #627

 When a variable needed for gradient computation has been modified by an in-place operation, Pytorch `torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly` prints `traceback` with a **line number** for variable in question that "was changed in there or anywhere later". For example:

```
with torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True):
        
  x = torch.rand(2, requires_grad = True)
  y = torch.rand(1)
  b = (x**y).sum()
  y.add_(1)
  b.backward()
```

Traceback says:
`line 12, in <module> b = (x**y).sum() 
`
to help identify error in `y.add_(1)`  for debugging into `y.add(1)`

Applying same code with R `with_detect_anomaly`
```
  with_detect_anomaly({
    
    x <- torch_rand(2, requires_grad = TRUE)
    y <- torch_rand(1)
    b <- (x^y)$sum()
    y$add_(1)
    b$backward()
    })
```
results in the following information:
`Warning: Error detected in PowBackward1. Traceback of forward call that caused the error:
000000006C7FC0E5 <unknown symbol address> R.dll!<unknown symbol> [<unknown file> @ <unknown line number>]`

It is difficult to debug with only `PowBackward1` information **(no line number)** for code that has many Pow operations. Shouldn't the traceback() provide line number and function where gradient computation failed `backward()`?

title: num_worker in dataloader opens many R sessions.
description:
Hi all,

I am trying to use torch with multiple cpu's, so that I can get results quicker.
To the best of my understanding, the current recommended way to use multiple cpu's is increasing num_worker in dataloader. Also, in the now-closed issue #467, the recommended way to do it is to not use torch tensors in dataset object. 
Two unexpected things happen when I follow the recommended way:
1- It takes ages to train the model compared to the single core case (num_workers = 0)
2- Many many R Sessions are created in the background and they all eat up RAM. 

Here is an example:

``` r
suppressWarnings(library(torch))
suppressWarnings(library(tidyverse))
suppressWarnings(library(palmerpenguins))
train_data <- penguins %>% 
  select(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm,flipper_length_mm,body_mass_g) %>% 
  as.matrix()
x_train <- train_data[,2:4]
y_train <- train_data[ ,1 ,drop = FALSE]
#x_train <- torch_tensor(x_train, dtype = torch_float())
#y_train <- torch_tensor(y_train, dtype = torch_float())
torch_dataset <- dataset(
  name = "my_data",
  initialize = function() {
    self$x_train <- x_train
    self$y_train <- y_train
  },
  .getitem = function(index) {
    x <- self$x_train[index, ]
    y <- self$y_train[index, ]
    list(x, y)
  },
  .length = function() {
    nrow(x_train)
  }
)

train_ds <- torch_dataset()
train_dl <- train_ds %>%
  dataloader(batch_size = 25, num_workers = 4L)


net = nn_module(
  "class_net",
  initialize = function(){
    self$linear1 = nn_linear(3,1)
  },
  forward = function(x){
    x %>%
      self$linear1() %>% 
      torch_squeeze()
  }
)
model = net()
optimizer <- optim_adam(model$parameters)

train_batch <- function(b) {
  
  optimizer$zero_grad()
  output <- model(b[[1]])
  target <- b[[2]]
  
  loss <- nnf_mse_loss(output, target)
  loss$backward()
  optimizer$step()
  
}
for (epoch in 1:50) {
  model$train()
  coro::loop(for (b in train_dl) {
    loss <-train_batch(b)
  })
}
```

title: Operations on high dimensional arrays
description:
I feel I must be missing something obvious here, but couldn't find a definitive answer in the docs.

Say I want to perform some operation on a higher (3+) order array. In base R, this is typically done via `apply.` For example,

``` r
(A = array(c(5,1,1,3), dim = c(2,2,2)))
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    5    1
#> [2,]    1    3
#> 
#> , , 2
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    5    1
#> [2,]    1    3

## One element example: Cholesky decomposition
chol(A[,,1])
#>          [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 2.236068 0.4472136
#> [2,] 0.000000 1.6733201

## Apply across all elements in the 3rd dimension
apply(A, 3, chol)
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 2.2360680 2.2360680
#> [2,] 0.0000000 0.0000000
#> [3,] 0.4472136 0.4472136
#> [4,] 1.6733201 1.6733201
```
Now, I convert to a Torch array and try the equivalent operation.

``` r
library(torch)

(At = torch_tensor(A))
#> torch_tensor
#> (1,.,.) = 
#>   5  5
#>   1  1
#> 
#> (2,.,.) = 
#>   1  1
#>   3  3
#> [ CPUFloatType{2,2,2} ]

## Single element works as (both encapsulated and functional methods)
At[,,1]$cholesky(upper = TRUE)
#> torch_tensor
#>  2.2361  0.4472
#>  0.0000  1.6733
#> [ CPUFloatType{2,2} ]
torch_cholesky(At[,,1], upper = TRUE)
#> torch_tensor
#>  2.2361  0.4472
#>  0.0000  1.6733
#> [ CPUFloatType{2,2} ]

## Vectorised(?) across the whole array doesn't work
At$cholesky()
#> Error in (function (self, upper) : cholesky_cpu: For batch 1: U(2,2) is zero, singular U.
#> Exception raised from batchCheckErrors at ../aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebraUtils.h:105 (most recent call first):
#> <... truncated error message ...>

## Fair enough, though apply + encapsulation doesn't work either
apply(At, 3, function(m) m$cholesky(upper = TRUE))
#> Error in m$cholesky: $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors

## The functional equivalent does
apply(At, 3, function(m) torch_cholesky(m, upper = TRUE))
#> [[1]]
#> torch_tensor
#>  2.2361  0.4472
#>  0.0000  1.6733
#> [ CPUFloatType{2,2} ]
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> torch_tensor
#>  2.2361  0.4472
#>  0.0000  1.6733
#> [ CPUFloatType{2,2} ]
```
I was (naively) hoping a "vectorised" solution might work out the box. However, it's nice to know that the `apply` + function approach carries over to tensor objects, even if the encapsulated methods don't.

Still, this presents a bit of a headache AFAICT when working with tensor arrays on a GPU. (Is there a functional way to convert to "cpu"? I apologise if I missed it.)

```r
## GPU
(Atg = torch_tensor(A, device = 'cuda'))
#> torch_tensor
#> (1,.,.) = 
#>   5  5
#>   1  1
#> 
#> (2,.,.) = 
#>   1  1
#>   3  3
#> [ CUDAFloatType{2,2,2} ]

## No dice for either approach
apply(Atg, 3, function(m) torch_cholesky(m, upper = TRUE))
#> Error: Can't convert cuda tensor to R. Convert to cpu tensor before.

apply(Atg, 3, function(m) torch_cholesky(m, upper = TRUE)$cpu())
#> Error: Can't convert cuda tensor to R. Convert to cpu tensor before.
```

A final approach that I tried is to combine the individual array matrices into a block diagonal matrix. This does work out of the tin, but now we're creating a sparse matrix that is sub-optimal from a memory perspective.

```r
## Block version
Ablock = torch_block_diag(list(A[,,1], A[,,2]))
Ablock$cholesky(upper = TRUE)
#> torch_tensor
#>  2.2361  0.4472  0.0000  0.0000
#>  0.0000  1.6733  0.0000  0.0000
#>  0.0000  0.0000  2.2361  0.4472
#>  0.0000  0.0000  0.0000  1.6733
#> [ CPUFloatType{4,4} ]
```

<sup>Created on 2021-07-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

Any pointers to the optimal way for performing operations on high(er) dimensional torch arrays would be much appreciated.

P.S Thanks for this fantastic package!

title: `jit_trace` strips names from lists of tensors
description:
I've been playing around with `jit_trace` for a package I'm working on. So far it is looking very useful but I ran into an issue when the function to be traced takes a named list of tensors and then uses the names inside the function. I was getting an esoteric error about `NULL` pointers. After a fair amount of debugging work I figured out the names are no longer accessible inside the function when using `jit_trace`. Here is a reprex, where I modify the example from your tests mentioned in #529:

``` r
library(torch)
#> Warning: package 'torch' was built under R version 4.0.3
```

This code works but the output has the name “res” stripped. Additionally we get a warning to be careful about returning a list in a traced function (see below).

``` r
fn <- function(x) { 
  list(res = torch_stack(list(x[[1]], x[[2]])))
} 
x <- list(t1 = torch_tensor(1), t2 = torch_tensor(2)) 

tr_fn <- jit_trace(fn, x)

tr_fn(x)
#> [[1]]
#> torch_tensor
#>  1
#>  2
#> [ CPUFloatType{2,1} ]
```

Running this version doesn’t work because names get stripped. This gives an esoteric error about an external pointer, but getting a `NULL` instead. Printing the names of the input shows that the names are now `NULL`.

``` r
fn <- function(x) {
  print(names(x))
  list(res = torch_stack(list(x$t1, x$t2)))
} 
x <- list(t1 = torch_tensor(1), t2 = torch_tensor(2)) 

tr_fn <- jit_trace(fn, x) 
#> NULL
#> Error in cpp_trace_function(tr_fn, ex_inp$ptr, .compilation_unit): Evaluation error: Expecting an external pointer: [type=NULL]..
```

The function itself works as expected:

``` r
fn(x)
#> [1] "t1" "t2"
#> $res
#> torch_tensor
#>  1
#>  2
#> [ CPUFloatType{2,1} ]
```

<sup>Created on 2021-04-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

<details style="margin-bottom:10px;">

<summary>Standard output and standard error</summary>

``` sh
[W ..\..\torch\csrc\jit\frontend\tracer.cpp:928] Warning: Encountering a list at the output of the tracer might cause the trace to be incorrect, this is only valid if the container structure does not change based on the module's inputs. Consider using a constant container instead (e.g. for `list`, use a `tuple` instead. for `dict`, use a `NamedTuple` instead). If you absolutely need this and know the side effects, pass strict=False to trace() to allow this behavior. (function defaultWarn)
```


</details>


This issue is fairly easy to workaround in most cases, but it is slightly annoying to not be able to refer to names.

transform_E <- function(mod_ts,Y,K, tau=50,lr=0.001, max_iter=10000){

      Chat = T_tensor$matmul(exp_E)

      L = (-Y*torch_log(Chat)+ (Y+tau)*torch_log(Chat+tau))$sum()/D
      return(L)
    }
  )
  T_tensor = calculate_T_ts(mod_ts)$clone()
  E0 = torch_randn(c(K, D), device=device)

    }
    optimizer$zero_grad()
    new_loss = tmp_E(Y,T_tensor, tau=tau, anno_dims=anno_dims)
    new_loss$backward()

Y <- torch_tensor(c(rep(1, 5), rep(0, 5)))

title: .getbatch should take a integer vector not a list
Deprecate the `enumerate` construct
description:
The `enumerate` construct will be deprecated in the next version of torch.

The main reason is that this object can cause very hard to debug errors when used incorrectly, for example if one does the following, the result is completely unexpected.

``` r
library(torch)
ds <- tensor_dataset(x = torch_randn(4))
dl <- dataloader(ds, batch_size = 2, shuffle = FALSE)

e <- enumerate(dl)
e[[2]]$x
#> torch_tensor
#> -0.8984
#> -0.6619
#> [ CPUFloatType{2} ]
for(b in e) {
  print(b$x)
}
#> torch_tensor
#> -1.0133
#>  1.9691
#> [ CPUFloatType{2} ]
#> torch_tensor
#> -1.0133
#>  1.9691
#> [ CPUFloatType{2} ]
```

Besides that, the active binding way of work in enumerate causes bugs when used within the RStudio IDE. See for example #457 .

We now favor the `coro::loop()` syntax. All `enumerate` usages can be changed to use:

```
coro::loop(for (batch in dl) {
  # do batch operation
})
```

Notes:

- No longer use `enumerate`.
- Wrap the `for` loop into `coro::loop()`.

title: JIT tracing functions with multiple parameters
description:
Currently we can't trace functions with multiple parameters, e.g., something like

```
fn1 <- function(x, y) {
    x + y
}
```
The issue I think stems from https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/88700be25bc0b1d7747d3a950570595922d11fef/tests/testthat/test-trace.R#L105-L115 where we support functions that take a list, which requires push the tensor list to the stack in one go here https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/88700be25bc0b1d7747d3a950570595922d11fef/R/trace.R#L57-L62

While the user could rewrite the function `fn1` to take a list, it's a bit unnatural especially in more complex examples. Also, some deployment targets (RedisAI for one) expect tensors and not lists thereof, so they would be blocked. Finally, the PyTorch example follows the pattern of treating `example_inputs` as an arg list (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.jit.trace.html)

```
import torch

def foo(x, y):
    return 2 * x + y

# Run `foo` with the provided inputs and record the tensor operations
traced_foo = torch.jit.trace(foo, (torch.rand(3), torch.rand(3)))
```

Could we consider modifying the behavior of `jit_trace()` so we treat `example_inputs` as an arg list?

title: in nnf_multi_head_attention_forward, return attention weights for each head
description:
Currently, the function averages the attention weights over all the heads before returning:
https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/d5cecbf342c857a0fbe9a5a29a09daf1441a706f/R/nnf-activation.R#L733

I'm not sure when it would be useful to have the average, but that's clearly the intended behavior. This function would be more useful to me if it returned the un-averaged weights, i.e.:

`  return(list(attn_output, attn_output_weights)) `
rather than
`  return(list(attn_output, attn_output_weights$sum(dim = 2)/num_heads)) `

Is there any reason *not* to make this change?

I see there's a discussion in pytorch about this, also:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/47583

I suppose there's a desire to keep torch as parallel to pytorch as possible. What's the policy about making changes in torch before they're made in pytorch?

title: Runtime
description:
Hi all,
first of all, I am very excited about this project because I’m already using pytorch in my own R package (via the torch pip wheel) and the prospect to use torch natively without the python intermediate step is very appealing.

I use pytorch more for smaller statistical models (datasets can still be very large) where the overhead plays an important role (e.g. the reimplementation of my core model in my pkg from R6 classes with the imported torch python module (via reticulate) to native python classes which are then imported into R via reticulate::import_from_path reduced the runtime on average by 30%, even for large datasets).

I compared r-torch, python-torch (written in python and imported into R), and imported-torch (torch was imported into R and code was written in R) by fitting a small neural network with 4 layers (4 layers, in sum 450 weights) and benchmarking the training loop. I found that the native python implementation is 20x times faster than the r-torch loop and even the imported torch training loop is 5x times faster than the r-torch loop:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/29951520/94696507-65be7f80-0337-11eb-83a8-bdbc21a34972.png)
(millisenconds)
Do have any ideas why the torch pkg is so much slower for smaller networks (at least I assume that this applies only for small models)?

R-Torch Code:
```
library(torch)
set.seed(1)

X = matrix(1.0, 200, 20)
Y = matrix(0.5, 200, 1)

net = nn_module(
  initialize = function() {
      self$fc1 = nn_linear(20, 10)
      self$fc2 = nn_linear(10, 10)
      self$fc3 = nn_linear(10, 10)
      self$fc4 = nn_linear(10, 1)
  },
  
  forward = function(x) {
    x %>% 
      self$fc1() %>%
      nnf_relu() %>%
      self$fc2() %>%
      nnf_relu() %>%
      self$fc3() %>%
      nnf_relu() %>%
      self$fc4()
  }
)
model <- net()
opt = optim_adam(model$parameters)
XT = torch_tensor(X, dtype=torch_float32())
YT = torch_tensor(Y, dtype=torch_float32())

result = 
    microbenchmark::microbenchmark({

        for(i in 1:50) {
            opt$zero_grad()
            pred = model(XT)
            loss = nnf_mse_loss(pred, YT)
            loss$backward()
            opt$step()
        }
    })
```

imported torch:
```
library(reticulate)
torch = import("torch")
set.seed(1)

X = matrix(1.0, 200, 20)
Y = matrix(0.5, 200, 1)

nn = torch$nn

model = nn$Sequential(
  (nn$Linear(20L, 10L)),
  (nn$ReLU()),
  (nn$Linear(10L, 10L)),
  (nn$ReLU()),
  (nn$Linear(10L, 10L)),
  (nn$ReLU()),
  (nn$Linear(10L, 1L))
)

XT = torch$tensor(X, dtype = torch$float32)
YT = torch$tensor(Y, dtype = torch$float32)

opt = torch$optim$Adam(model$parameters())

result = 
    microbenchmark::microbenchmark({
            for(i in 1:50) {
                opt$zero_grad()
                pred = model(XT)
                loss = torch$nn$functional$mse_loss(pred, YT)
                loss$backward()
                opt$step()
            }
    })
```

Native python:
A) python part
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(Net, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(20, 10)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(10, 10)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(10, 10)
        self.fc4 = nn.Linear(10, 1)

    def forward(self, X):
        x = F.relu( self.fc1(X) )
        x = F.relu( self.fc2(x) )
        x = F.relu( self.fc3(x) )
        x = self.fc4(x)
        return x

class Train:
    def __init__(self):
        self.net = Net()
    
    def train(self, X, Y):
        opt = torch.optim.Adam(self.net.parameters())

        for i in range(50):
            opt.zero_grad()
            Pred = self.net(X)
            loss = F.mse_loss(Pred, Y)
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()

```
B) R part:
```
library(reticulate)
torch = import("torch")
set.seed(1)

X = matrix(1.0, 200, 20)
Y = matrix(0.5, 200, 1)

py_torch = reticulate::import_from_path("python", "python/")
net = py_torch$Train()
XT = torch$tensor(X, dtype = torch$float32)
YT = torch$tensor(Y, dtype = torch$float32)

result = 
    microbenchmark::microbenchmark({
        net$train(XT, YT)
    })

```

title: Post-install script downloading shared libraries fails in multi-user environment (Linux)
description:
### Problem:

##### installation (as superuser):
install.packages("torch", "/usr/local/lib/R/site-library")

##### then run (as standard user)
library("torch")

##### this downloads shared libraries then fails
Failed to install Torch, manually run install_torch(). 


### Cause of the problem

A standard user has no write access to torch:::install_path()
In the above this is "/usr/local/lib/R/site-library/torch//deps"
Only the superuser can do this.


### Solution

#### Install as superuser as follows:

install.packages("torch", "/usr/local/lib/R/site-library")
torch::install_torch()   

Therefore, please amend the installation instructions correspondingly at
https://torch.mlverse.org/docs/ and https://torch.mlverse.org/packages/#installation-and-use


### Better solution:

Run the torch::install_torch() as post-install script automatically
whenever install.packages() is called.

However, I am not sure this is actually supported by install.packages()

Failed to install Torch, manually run install_torch(). /home/mbergins/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/3.6/torch/deps/liblantern.so - libnvToolsExt.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory 
> install_torch()
Error in cpp_lantern_init(normalizePath(install_path())) : 
  /home/mbergins/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/3.6/torch/deps/liblantern.so - libnvToolsExt.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
```
The shared object file libnvToolsExt was present in the same deps directory though, it just appears that the appropriate simlink was missing. I fixed this with:

`ln -s libnvToolsExt-3965bdd0.so.1 libnvToolsExt.so.1`

I'm also assuming that this link should exist, but was missed in the installation. Same problem with another shared library file:

```
> install_torch()
Error in cpp_lantern_init(normalizePath(install_path())) : 
  /home/mbergins/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/3.6/torch/deps/liblantern.so - libcudart.so.10.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
```
Once again fixed by adding a symlink in deps:

`ln -s libcudart-1b201d85.so.10.1 libcudart.so.10.1`

Everything else has gone smoothly, but wanted to point out this small speed bump I encountered. I'm not sure if there is anything to fix in the library, but wanted to make a post somewhere in case another Ubuntu (or other OS, I suppose) user hits the same problem.

Thanks for your work bring machine learning tools to R, looking forward to writing some code with torch.

title: speedup rnns on gpu
description:
Currently we get the following warning when using rnn's on the gpu:

```
[W RNN.cpp:775] Warning: RNN module weights are not part of single contiguous chunk of memory. This means they need to be compacted at every call, possibly greatly increasing memory usage. To compact weights again call flatten_parameters(). (function _cudnn_rnn)

In order to fix it we need to implement the `flatten_parameters()` method here:

https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/6ae289dc5ee0271156083bcf650126b96d8b5581/R/nn-rnn.R#L108

For this, we need to port:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a38a648cb7b900374a5c4b8bf3e7b17a64981727/torch/nn/modules/rnn.py#L130-L134

title: requires_grad becomes TRUE after to(device = "cpu")
description:
Hi! If I set requires_grad_(FALSE) and then call to(device = "cpu"), requires_grad() will become TRUE again. Reprex follows:

``` r
library(torch)

# nn_modules NOT OK ------------------------------------------ 
x <- nn_linear(1,1)
x$weight$requires_grad 
#> [1] TRUE

x$weight$requires_grad_(FALSE)
#> torch_tensor

x$weight$requires_grad
#> [1] FALSE

x$to(device = "cpu")
x$weight$requires_grad

x$requires_grad 
#> [1] TRUE

x$requires_grad_(FALSE)
