title: Hidden unit permutation incompatible with current LSTM output
description:
I noticed that LSTM breaks with packed sequences, e.g.
```
x <- torch_tensor(rbind(
  c(1, 2, 0, 0),
  c(1, 2, 3, 0),
  c(1, 2, 3, 4)
), dtype = torch_float())
x <- x[,,newaxis]
lens <- torch_tensor(c(2,3,4), dtype = torch_long())
  
p <- nn_utils_rnn_pack_padded_sequence(x, lens, batch_first = TRUE, 
                                       enforce_sorted = FALSE)
x
rnn <- nn_lstm(1, 4)
out <- rnn(p)
```
gives
```
Error in nn_apply_permutation(hx, permutation) : 
  attempt to apply non-function
```
This is due to https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/0555381cc1ff3fcbb76f36329811124daf18c920/R/nn-rnn.R#L203 where we assume that `hidden` is a tensor, but is actually a list in this scenario. One approach would be to concat the list along the batch dimension before permuting, but if we do so, we would need to split the result before returning, since we're enforcing the current structure here https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/0555381cc1ff3fcbb76f36329811124daf18c920/tests/testthat/test-nn-rnn.R#L98

I'd like to confirm the desired structure of the hidden output for LSTM/GRU before sending a fix for this use case.

title: Training Loss Different GPU vs. CPU
description:
First off, thank you for the work that you all have done bringing `torch` to the R ecosystem. I've been wanting to try `torch` to supplement my `tensorflow`/`keras` deep learning with it for a while.

This issue may be due mostly to my ignorance of torch, but some Googling appears that others have experienced similar issues using `pytorch` and it is an unexpected behavior. Basically, I am trying to run a modified version of the example ("Guess the Correlation") and I get substantially different training losses when the only variable that has changed is `device = "cpu"` vs `device = "cuda"`. You can see the difference over 5 epochs below:

## GPU Training:

    Loss at epoch 1: training: 0.40000, validation: 0.38992

    Loss at epoch 2: training: 0.40521, validation: 0.40653
                                                                              
    Loss at epoch 3: training: 0.39901, validation: 0.39910

    Loss at epoch 4: training: 0.39461, validation: 0.39970
    
    Loss at epoch 5: training: 0.39562, validation: 0.38798

## CPU Training

    Loss at epoch 1: training: 0.13443, validation: 0.03077
    
    Loss at epoch 2: training: 0.01498, validation: 0.21862
    
    Loss at epoch 3: training: 0.01070, validation: 0.06492
    
    Loss at epoch 4: training: 0.00921, validation: 0.18520
    
    Loss at epoch 5: training: 0.00795, validation: 0.49545

I thought it may be due to an outdated NVIDIA driver, but I updated my driver and CUDA and the issue persisted (see info below). I am running this in a Docker container, but I have upgraded Docker to the latest version as well (though I don't see why that should affect this).

If this is a known phenomenon with Lantern, I apologize. However, if not, I would appreciate any ideas debugging the issue! Full script and GPU/CPU info below.

## Script
```{r eval = FALSE}
library(torch)
library(torchvision)
library(torchdatasets)

# device = "cpu"
device = "cuda"

# Get the datasets ----
train_indices <- 1:10000
val_indices <- 10001:15000
test_indices <- 15001:20000

add_channel_dim <- function(img) img$unsqueeze(1)
crop_axes <- function(img) transform_crop(img, top = 0, left = 21, height = 131, width = 130)

root <- file.path("data", "correlation")

train_ds <- guess_the_correlation_dataset(
  # where to unpack
  root = root,
  # additional preprocessing 
  transform = function(img) crop_axes(img) %>% add_channel_dim(),
  # don't take all data, but just the indices we pass in
  indexes = train_indices,
  download = TRUE
)

valid_ds <- guess_the_correlation_dataset(
  root = root,
  transform = function(img) crop_axes(img) %>% add_channel_dim(),
  indexes = val_indices,
  download = FALSE
)

test_ds <- guess_the_correlation_dataset(
  root = root,
  transform = function(img) crop_axes(img) %>% add_channel_dim(),
  indexes = test_indices,
  download = FALSE
)

# Work with batches ----
train_dl <- dataloader(train_ds, batch_size = 64, shuffle = TRUE)
batch <- dataloader_make_iter(train_dl) %>% dataloader_next()

par(mfrow = c(8,8), mar = rep(0, 4))

images <- as.array(batch$x$squeeze(2))

images %>%
  purrr::array_tree(1) %>%
  purrr::map(as.raster) %>%
  purrr::iwalk(~{plot(.x)})

valid_dl <- dataloader(valid_ds, batch_size = 64)
test_dl <- dataloader(test_ds, batch_size = 64)

# Create the model ----
torch_manual_seed(777)

net <- nn_module(
  
  "corr-cnn",
  
  initialize = function() {
    
    self$conv1 <- nn_conv2d(in_channels = 1, out_channels = 32, kernel_size = 3)
    self$conv2 <- nn_conv2d(in_channels = 32, out_channels = 64, kernel_size = 3)
    self$conv3 <- nn_conv2d(in_channels = 64, out_channels = 128, kernel_size = 3)
    
    self$bn1 <- nn_batch_norm2d(num_features = 32)
    self$bn2 <- nn_batch_norm2d(num_features = 64)
    self$bn3 <- nn_batch_norm2d(num_features = 128)
    self$bn4 <- nn_batch_norm1d(num_features = 128)
    
    self$fc1 <- nn_linear(in_features = 14 * 14 * 128, out_features = 128)
    self$fc2 <- nn_linear(in_features = 128, out_features = 1)
    
  },
  
  forward = function(x) {
    
    x %>% 
      self$conv1() %>%
      nnf_relu() %>%
      self$bn1() %>%
      nnf_avg_pool2d(2) %>%
      nnf_dropout(p = 0.2) %>%
      
      self$conv2() %>%
      nnf_relu() %>%
      self$bn2() %>%
      nnf_avg_pool2d(2) %>%
      nnf_dropout(p = 0.2) %>%
      
      self$conv3() %>%
      nnf_relu() %>%
      self$bn3() %>%
      nnf_avg_pool2d(2) %>%
      nnf_dropout(p = 0.2) %>%
      
      torch_flatten(start_dim = 2) %>%
      self$fc1() %>%
      nnf_relu() %>%
      self$bn4() %>%
      
      self$fc2()
  }
)

model <- net()

# Train the network ----
optimizer <- optim_adam(model$parameters)

train_batch <- function(b) {
  
  optimizer$zero_grad()
  
  # get predictions
  output <- model(b$x$to(device = device))
  
  # calculate loss
  loss <- nnf_mse_loss(output, b$y$unsqueeze(2)$to(device = device))
  
  # have gradients get calculated        
  loss$backward()
  
  # have gradients get applied
  optimizer$step()
  
  loss$item()
  
}

valid_batch <- function(b) {
  
  output <- model(b$x$to(device = device))
  loss <- nnf_mse_loss(output, b$y$unsqueeze(2)$to(device = device))
  loss$item()
  
}

model <- model$to(device = device)

num_epochs <- 5

for (epoch in 1:num_epochs) {
  
  cat("\nEpoch: ", epoch)
  
  # don't forget to do this
  model$train()
  
  train_losses <- c()
  
  pb <- progress::progress_bar$new(
    total = length(train_dl),
    format = " Training [:bar] :current/:total (:percent)"
    )
  for (b in enumerate(train_dl)) {
    pb$tick()
    loss <- train_batch(b)
    train_losses <- c(train_losses, loss)
    
  }
  
  # don't forget to do this either
  model$eval()
  
  valid_losses <- c()
  
  pb <- progress::progress_bar$new(
    total = length(valid_dl),
    format = " Validation [:bar] :current/:total (:percent)"
  )
  for (b in enumerate(valid_dl)) {
    pb$tick()
    loss <- valid_batch(b)
    valid_losses <- c(valid_losses, loss)
    
  }
  
  cat(sprintf("\nLoss at epoch %d: training: %1.5f, validation: %1.5f\n",
              epoch, mean(train_losses), mean(valid_losses)))
  
}
```

title: Intel optimizations?
description:
From what I understand there are [three ](https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/articles/getting-started-with-intel-optimization-of-pytorch.html) separate intel-related improvements to pytorch:
- oneDNN: optimizations built into (?) the current release of pytorch
- IPEX: intel "extensions" for pytorch
- oneCCL: for multi-node (?) distributed learning

Here's a good (recent) overview of these improvements:
https://medium.com/pytorch/accelerate-pytorch-with-ipex-and-onednn-using-intel-bf16-technology-dca5b8e6b58f

I'm guessing that using IPEX and oneCCL are not currently usable with torch in R, and I'm unsure whether oneDNN optimizations are incorporated (do they depend on python code? or just c++? Or are they only turned on via settings in IPEX?).  

Can you comment on whether you have plans on bringing in some of these optimizations?  I think there's probably a lot of researchers in the R community that would benefit from from these optimizations given universities tend to have large CPU-based HPC clusters.

It would also be nice to know whether getting intel optimizations working is a higher priority here or in tensorflow (https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/issues/453). My vote would be here, in torch, since the native solution is likely to work better.

title: Extending the "Serialization" Vignette for loading models saved in Python
description:
Hi - I am attempting to develop code to use models trained in Python via PyTorch read into R with the end product being a Shiny application to use these models via Rtorch for predictions. As a first step, I need to read a .pt file into R. 

I have played around with the example provided in the Serialization vignette and I am using the Alexnet example as a starting point [see here](https://github.com/mlverse/torchvision/blob/main/R/models-alexnet.R#L2-L63)

Unfortunately the R portion of my code seems to fail. I am hoping I can get this simple example to work, then make a request to add this in order to have a full example in the "Serialization" vignette.

I am new to this, so I apologize if there is a stupid error in here somewhere. 

Python Code:

```
import torch
import numpy as np

#Make up data
madeUpData_x = np.random.rand(1000,100)
madeUpData_y = np.random.rand(1000,1)
madeUpData_y = madeUpData_y.round()
train_py_X = torch.from_numpy(madeUpData_x).float()

train_py_Y = torch.from_numpy(madeUpData_y).float()


class simpleMLP(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(simpleMLP, self).__init__()
        self.modelFit = torch.nn.Sequential(
            torch.nn.Linear(100,20),
            torch.nn.ReLU(),
            torch.nn.Linear(20,1),
            torch.nn.Sigmoid()
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        x =self.modelFit(x)

        return x

model = simpleMLP()

def modelTrainer(data_X,data_Y,model):
    criterion = torch.nn.BCELoss()
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.001, momentum=0.9)

    for epoch in range(100):

        optimizer.zero_grad()

        yhat = model(data_X)

        loss = criterion(yhat,data_Y.unsqueeze(1))

        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

modelTrainer(data_X = train_py_X,data_Y = train_py_Y,model = model)

#-----------------------------------------------------------------
#save the model 

torch.save(model,f="yourPath/babyTest.pt",
           _use_new_zipfile_serialization=True)


```

R Code: 

```

library(torch)
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------


simpleMLP <- torch::nn_module(
  "simpleMLP",
  initialize = function(){
    
    self$modelFit <- nn_sequential(nn_linear(100,20),
                                   nn_relu(),
                                   nn_linear(20,1),
                                   nn_sigmoid())
    
  },
  forward = function(x){
    
    x <- self$modelFit
    return(x)
    
  }
)

model_JAL <- function() {
  
  model <- simpleMLP()
  
  
  state_dict_path <- "path/babyTest.pt"
  
  state_dict <- torch::load_state_dict(state_dict_path)
  model$load_state_dict(state_dict)
  
  
  model
}

```

The R part of the code that fails is the torch::load_state_dict(). I assume there is an error in the creation of the class in R. I can run the AlexNet example just fine. 

I hope I made this reproducible, but if not please let me know.

title: please provide a `install_torch()` option that relies on local `file:/` URL
description:
Hello, 

### Current situation
`install_torch()` fails on air-gap networked server, as mentionned by @dirkschumacher in https://github.com/mlverse/torch/issues/267#issuecomment-716711696_.

### Possible improvement
In order to install `libtorch` and `liblantern` on air-gapped server, we can usually rely on zip files uploaded on the machine filesystem. 

Could we have an `install_torch()` option or an alternative command like `install_torch_from_file()` that relies on local filesystem zip files ?

### Workaround
As a current hack to this, it is possible (but not convenient) to manually change the files URL to local files, as `utils::download.file()` that is used behind the scene supports `files://` prefixed url: 
1 - copy the repository `R/install.R` file in a local R session
2- edit the content of `install_config` list on line 4 with file urls turned into  `file://...` entries : 
In my very personnal case it turn out to be
```(r)
install_config <- list(
  "1.7.1" = list(
    "cpu" = list(
      "darwin" = list(
        "libtorch" = list(
          url = "file:///Users/to9444/Downloads/libtorch-macos-1.7.1.zip",
          path = "libtorch/lib",
          filter = ".dylib",
          md5hash = "d1d0561fa91326afcb7f0abe0241e704"
        ),
        "liblantern" = "file:///Users/to9444/Downloads/macOS.zip"
      )
    )
  )
)
```

title: Building lantern with CUDA and existing libtorch
description:
I'll split this in three sections: 

- allowing for existing libtorch to be used when building lantern
- bug in pytorch cmake config
- allowing for existing libtorch to be used when installing torch

1. We could allow people to specify a LIBTORCH_DIR and pass that as DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH to cmake  in `buildlantern.R`.
   Here I'm hardcoding it, but it could be an env var:

```
withr::with_dir("lantern/build", {
    system("cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/home/key/libtorch ..")
    # ...
  })
```

2. I'm running into the same Pytorch-level bug in cmake config I documented here:

https://github.com/mlverse/torch/issues/3
https://github.com/mlverse/lantern/issues/11

Basically this will only happen to people who don't have stuff in `/usr/local/cuda` - but still, it is a bug that, it seems, was never resolved in Pytorch: see https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/libtorch-cmake-issues/28246/7.

My workaround are the two lines between the calls to cmake, here:

```
withr::with_dir("lantern/build", {
    system("cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/home/key/libtorch ..")
    system("sed -i 's;/local/cuda;;g' CMakeFiles/lantern.dir/build.make")
    system("sed -i 's;/local/cuda;;g' CMakeFiles/example-app.dir/link.txt")
    system("cmake --build . --target lantern --config Release --parallel 8")  
  })
```

3. With those above changes, `install_torch` in `buildlantern.R` will run, but it will download the 800M zip for nothing ... 
I would suggest that if a user has `LIBTORCH_DIR`, we directly copy the libs from there.

title: use nvcc -- version instead of nvidia-smi to detect installed CUDA version (Linux)
description:
On Linux 
https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/master/R/install.R
uses the command "nvidia-smi" to detect the installed CUDA version.  However this returns the highest CUDA version that the installed graphics driver is capable to support, not the actually installed version of CUDA!  The installed version is obtained by running the command "nvcc --version":

The CUDA version in Debian 10 is 10.1:
https://packages.debian.org/buster-backports/nvidia-cuda-toolkit

This gives the correct version:
> nvcc --version
nvcc: NVIDIA (R) Cuda compiler driver
Copyright (c) 2005-2019 NVIDIA Corporation
Built on Sun_Jul_28_19:07:16_PDT_2019
Cuda compilation tools, release 10.1, V10.1.243


This gives the wrong version (it shows the CUDA version the driver version 450.66 is able to support)
> nvidia-smi
...    
| NVIDIA-SMI 450.66       Driver Version: 450.66       CUDA Version: 11.0     |
....

See also:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53422407/different-cuda-versions-shown-by-nvcc-and-nvidia-smi

title: Working with torch dataset abstract class
description:
Hi @dfalbel,

I am running into a couple issues when creating a custom `dataset` and `dataloader` and wanted to see if I'm doing something wrong. The documentation suggests that when creating a `dataset` that one should overwrite the `length()` and `get_item()` methods, but I get some locking errors when I try this. 
> All datasets that represent a map from keys to data samples should subclass it. All subclasses should overwrite get_item, supporting fetching a data sample for a given key. Subclasses could also optionally overwrite lenght, which is expected to return the size of the dataset

However, I can overwrite `.length()` and `.getitem()` without issue. Am I doing something wrong? I am somewhat new to the whole `PyTorch` API so I may just have an incorrect mental model of how this should work...

See example below:
``` r
library(torch)
library(tidyverse)
library(rsample)

split <- initial_split(mtcars)

ds <- 
  dataset(
  split = split,
  initialize = function(set = "train") {
    type = switch(
      set,
      train = training(self$split),
      valid = testing(self$split)
      )
    self$data <- type
    self$length <- function() nrow(self$data)
    self$get_item <- function(i) self$data[i, ]
  }
)
ds(set = "train")
#> Error in self$get_item <- function(i) self$data[i, ]: cannot change value of locked binding for 'get_item'
ds(set = "valid")

  dataset(
    split = split,
    initialize = function(set = "train") {
      type = switch(
        set,
        train = training(self$split),
        valid = testing(self$split)
      )
      self$data <- type
      self$.length <- function() nrow(self$data)
      self$.getitem <- function(i) self$data[i, ]
    }
  )
train <- ds2(set = "train")
train
#> <dataset>
#>   Public:
#>     .getitem: function (i)

#>     add: function (other) 
#>     clone: function (deep = FALSE)

train$.length()

train$.getitem(1)

dataloader(ds2(), batch_size = 16, collate_fn = bind_rows)$.iter()$.next()

title: inconsistency in size() output
description:
There is an inconsistency in `size()` output depending whether you're calling it on the result returned from indexing or a newly created tensor:

```
> t[1, 1]$size()
integer(0)

> torch_tensor(1)$size()
[1] 1
```

In Python, the latter case results in an empty list as well as the former:

```
>>> torch.tensor(1).size()
torch.Size([])
```

If you asked me, I'd actually prefer making this consistent by NOT doing what Python does - to me, returning a size of `1` in both cases seems intuitive...

title: GPU support on Windows
description:
Currently we are not supporting CUDA on Windows. 
The main step to be solved is to be able to correctly build lantern on windows with GPU support. 

The entrypoint is to tweak the CMake file here: https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/master/lantern/CMakeLists.txt#L40-L41

Then, we need to add the GPU build in the GH actions that generates pre-build lantern binaries here: https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/master/.github/workflows/lantern.yaml

We can then tweak the download links here: https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/master/R/install.R#L31-L56

title: Truncate vector when printing
description:
Hi! thanks for this awesome package. Really useful!

One minor issue that I've stumbled upon is that when I print a big tensor, it prints all the elements of it, which takes a lot of time.

For example:

```r
library(torch)
s <- seq_len(1e6)
torch_tensor(matrix(s, ncol = 1e3))
```

I think we should truncate the output someway. Maybe only the first 20~30 lines (controlling by the `n=` parameter from the `print()` method) + the last line to show the dimensions of the tensor.

title: Developing CPU/GPU/TPU at home and on Colab - Question
description:
When exploring at home, which is only CPU capable, library(torch) downloads  CPU deps, and Lantern CPU build. Without specifying a runtime on Colab (which is to say CPU), GPU deps are downloaded. Changing Colab runtime to TPU still results in GPU download. 

Through the course of this experimenting, and reviewing runtime logs along the way, source of deps changes: google.storageapis on Colab and pytorch.org CPU at home. 

All this suggests a sophisticated, environment aware switch. Is it anticipated, going forward, a devtools::install_github('mlverse/torch', type = c('CPU','GPU','TPU')), for a given runtime under consideration.

Thanks.

title: Serialize torch objects to raw vectors in memory?
description: It would be great to have an injective transformation from `torch` objects to exportable raw vector in memory, just like `serialize_model()` and `unserialize_model()` in `keras`. This would allow folks like me to build native `torch` data support for pipeline tools that send in-memory data over a network to distributed workers (e.g. [`targets`](https://github.com/wlandau/targets) and possibly [`drake`](https://github.com/ropensci/drake)). Ref: https://github.com/wlandau/targets/issues/179. Apologies if I missed something obvious.

import numpy as np

title: pack_padded_sequence / pad_packed_sequence
description:
I've been trying to reproduce this https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/nlp/sequence_models_tutorial.html
Using the development version of the sentencepiece package to get embeddings

That seems to work. Some features before I could build this are functionalities to increase the batch_size. For this I think what is needed is pack_padded_sequence / pad_packed_sequence?
Any chance to put this on your timeline?

```
library(sentencepiece) #remotes::install_github("bnosac/sentencepiece")
library(word2vec) # from CRAN
library(torch)
downloads <- sentencepiece_download_model("english", vocab_size = 25000, dim = 25, model_dir = getwd())
bpemb <- BPEembed(file_sentencepiece = downloads$file_model,
                  file_word2vec = downloads$glove.bin$file_model)

##
## DOCS AT https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/nlp/sequence_models_tutorial.html
##
ner_bilstm <- nn_module(
  classname = "ner_bilstm",
  initialize = function(bpemb, tagset_size, hidden_size = 32, num_layers = 1, seq_len = 100) {
    self$bpemb          <- bpemb
    self$embedding_dim  <- bpemb$dim
    self$seq_len        <- seq_len
    self$tagset_size    <- as.integer(tagset_size)
    self$num_layers     <- as.integer(num_layers)
    self$hidden_size    <- as.integer(hidden_size)
    
    ## LSTM Layer
    self$rnn       <- nn_rnn(mode = "LSTM", input_size = self$embedding_dim, 
                             hidden_size = self$hidden_size, num_layers = self$num_layers,
                             dropout = 0, bidirectional = TRUE, nonlinearity = "tanh", batch_first = TRUE)
    ## Map of LSTM features to tag space
    self$linear    <- nn_linear(in_features = hidden_size * 2, out_features = tagset_size, bias = TRUE)
  },
  forward = function(tokensequence) {
    # current implementation only works for 1 tokensequence at a time
    batch_size <- 1L 

    ## Tokenize and get the embedding of the tokens - sentencepiece splits according to subwords, take the average embedding of the subwords
    emb <- predict(self$bpemb, newdata = tokensequence, type = "encode")
    emb <- lapply(emb, colMeans)
    emb <- do.call(rbind, emb)
    
    ## Pad zeros to the maximum length of the text sequence + put these in a tensor
    #emb <- rbind(emb, matrix(0, nrow = seq_len - nrow(emb), ncol = ncol(emb)))
    n_tokens <- nrow(emb)

    ## Forward pass, geting the LSTM features
    emb <- torch_tensor(emb, dtype = torch_float())
    emb <- torch_reshape(emb, list(batch_size, -1, self$embedding_dim)) 
    #rnn_out <- self$rnn(emb)
    rnn_out <- self$rnn(emb, torch_zeros(self$num_layers * 2, batch_size, self$hidden_size, dtype = emb$dtype()))
    rnn_out <- rnn_out[[1]]
    
    ## Put the LSTM feature in 1 line per token and do a Forward pass over the linear layer 
    rnn_out <- torch_reshape(rnn_out, list(n_tokens, -1)) 
    tag_space <- self$linear(rnn_out)
    
    ## Softmax by token, output is 1 line per token with as many columns as there are labels to predict
    tag_scores <- torch_reshape(tag_space, list(-1, self$tagset_size))
    nnf_log_softmax(tag_scores, dim = 1L)
  }
)
traindata <- list(
  data.frame(doc_id = 1, 
             token = c("the", "dog", "ate", "the", "apple"),
             entity = c("DET", "NN", "V", "DET", "NN"),
             entity_nr = c(0, 1, 2, 0, 1), stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  data.frame(doc_id = 2, 
             token = c("everybody", "read", "that", "book"),
             entity = c("NN", "V", "DET", "NN"), 
             entity_nr = c(1, 2, 0, 1), stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
model <- ner_bilstm(bpemb = bpemb, tagset_size = 3, hidden_size = 8)

optimizer <- optim_sgd(model$parameters, lr = 0.1, momentum = 0.9)

for(epoch in 1:10){
  cat(sprintf("%s epoch %s", Sys.time(), epoch), sep = "\n")
  for(b in traindata){
    optimizer$zero_grad()
    tokens      <- b[["token"]]
    reality     <- b[["entity_nr"]]
    reality     <- torch_tensor(reality, dtype = torch_long())
    tag_scores  <- model(tokens)
    
    loss <- nnf_nll_loss(tag_scores, reality, ignore_index = -1)
    loss$backward()
    optimizer$step()
  }  
}
```

title: Structure of model parameters R vs P, and named_parameters()
description:
In Python, the following structure of parameters is hierarchical:

```{python}
model = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Linear(3, 16),
    torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Linear(16, 1),
)
```
Such that to access the first layer's bias, you'd say

```{python}
model[0].bias
```

In R, I get a (non-hierarchical) list:

```
model <- nn_sequential(
    nn_linear(3, 16),
    nn_relu(),
    nn_linear(16, 1),
)
model$parameters
```

This is not a problem as far as I can see now (just changes the way of access). Still, wanted to get your opinion if we could, and whether we should, keep it the Python way :-)

Related question: I noticed we don't have `named_parameters()`, the method I was using from Python. Here too I don't see why it should be indispensable, but still, wondering if we should have it.

title: Discussion: methods vs. function in R and Python
description:
Currently, with tensor modification, our strategy seems to be:

- R functions (`torch_`) only when a fresh object is returned
- R methods (`x$what()`) only when the existing object is modified

e.g. `tx$view()` but `torch_reshape`

I assume this is why I don't see an `x$clone()` 
(also I notice we have `x$t_()` but not `x$t()`)

But, a person coming from Python might expect `$` access to work independently of whether there are side effects or not (there is an `x.clone()`, etc.)

Not saying we have to follow this ... but partly we do: For example, there is `x$mm` as well as `x$mm_` in R ... 

What do you think?

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.0 FATAL_ERROR)
project(example-app)

find_package(Torch REQUIRED)
set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${TORCH_CXX_FLAGS}")

target_link_libraries(example-app "${TORCH_LIBRARIES}")

title: Tensor row slicing `x[i, ]` can misread the missing column index after garbage collection
description:
I encountered an intermittent out-of-bounds error while reading a tensor row in a dataloader. I can reproduce it in a fresh R session with a single dense CPU tensor. The example asks for row 3 of a 100 × 6 tensor. The error refers to the column dimension, even though the column index is blank.

```r
library(torch)

x <- torch_tensor(matrix(as.numeric(1:600), nrow = 100))

gc_row <- function(row) {
  gc()
  z <- vector("list", 150000L)
  # Allocate separate integer scalars, each containing 29.
  for (k in seq_along(z)) z[[k]] <- k - k + 29L
  row
}

as.numeric(x$select(1L, gc_row(3L)))
# [1] 3 103 203 303 403 503

as.numeric(x[gc_row(3L), ])
# Error: index 28 is out of bounds for dimension 1 with size 6
```

Both expressions should return all six values in row 3. The explicit `gc()` and allocations make the original intermittent failure reproducible on my machine.

One possible cause is the lifetime of the missing-index marker in [`evaluate_slices()`](https://github.com/mlverse/torch/blob/v0.17.0/src/indexing.cpp#L50-L71). It stores the temporary logical vector in a raw `SEXP`, then evaluates the row expression before using the marker for the blank column. Could the marker be collected during that evaluation? Keeping it in an `Rcpp::LogicalVector` for the duration of the loop may be sufficient.

Reproduced with R 4.6.2 and torch 0.17.0 on macOS (Apple Silicon), using the CPU.
